title: Rice Sheath Blight (Rhizoctonia solani AG-1 IA, teleomorph Thanatephorus cucumeris)
content: Rice sheath blight is the second most economically important fungal disease of cultivated rice (Oryza sativa L.) worldwide after rice blast, caused by the necrotrophic, soilborne, basidiomycetous fungus Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn anastomosis group AG-1 IA (teleomorph stage: Thanatephorus cucumeris (A.B. Frank) Donk, class Agaricomycetes, order Cantharellales, family Ceratobasidiaceae). The disease occurs in all major rice-growing regions of Asia, North and South America, Africa, Australia, and southern Europe; it is particularly severe in intensive, high-input, high-yielding irrigated lowland rice systems with high nitrogen fertilization and dense plant canopies. Annual grain yield losses of 10-30% are reported globally; in severe localized epidemics on susceptible indica rice cultivars under heavy nitrogen fertilization, yield losses of 50% and reductions of 20-40% in head rice milling recovery are documented. In addition to rice, R. solani AG-1 IA has a very wide host range of > 200 plant species in > 30 families including maize (Zea mays, banded leaf and sheath blight), soybean (Glycine max, aerial blight / Rhizoctonia foliar blight), sorghum, sugarcane, potato (stem canker and black scurf), tomato, eggplant, pepper, bean (Phaseolus vulgaris, web blight), cotton, peanut, turfgrasses, and many vegetable crops and weeds. Symptoms on rice first appear on the leaf sheaths of the lower (basal) canopy, typically at the maximum tillering to late booting growth stages (approximately 4-8 weeks after transplanting in irrigated lowland rice), as small (1-3 cm), elliptical to oval, water-soaked, grayish-green lesions with a distinct, narrow, dark brown to purple-black margin. As lesions expand, the central lesion portion becomes bleached, dried, papery, off-white to grayish-white, retaining only the characteristic dark brown margin; multiple adjacent lesions coalesce to form large, irregular, band-shaped, 'marbled' or 'tiger-striped' necrotic areas 5-30 cm long that typically encircle or girdle the lower leaf sheaths, causing the death of the entire leaf blade attached to the infected sheath. The diagnostic microscopic feature of R. solani AG-1 IA observed in lesion scrapings with a 10-40x compound microscope is the presence of coarse, brown, septate, vegetative hyphae 5-14 um in diameter with distinctive, acute, near-right-angle (80-90 degree) branching and a conspicuous septum and slight constriction ('branching constriction') at the point of origin of each lateral hyphal branch. Small (0.3-3.0 mm), irregularly shaped, lobed, compact, brown-to-black asexual survival structures called sclerotia are produced abundantly on the surfaces of heavily infected leaf sheaths, stems, and within leaf sheath cavities; sclerotia initially appear as white, cottony tufts of mycelium that rapidly darken to become hard, melanized, sand-grain-like structures after 3-5 days. Under humid, warm, still conditions, the basidial (teleomorphic, sexual) Thanatephorus cucumeris stage may form a thin, delicate, greyish-white, powdery hymenial layer on the surface of maturing lesions, producing microscopic 4-spored basidia and kidney-shaped basidiospores; however, the role of airborne basidiospores in sheath blight epidemiology is generally considered minor compared to the asexual mycelial and sclerotial stages. Severe sheath blight infections that grow upward from the basal leaf sheaths to infect the upper culm nodes and the panicle sheath ('flag leaf sheath infection' at heading) cause the most economically significant losses: panicle sheath infection results in incomplete grain filling, increased percentages of sterile unfilled spikelets ('blank heads'), chalky grain, reduced 1000-grain kernel weight, and significantly lower head rice recovery after milling. R. solani AG-1 IA is a soilborne pathogen that overwinters primarily as melanized sclerotia in the top 0-10 cm of soil and in the form of dormant mycelium in infected rice crop residue (rice stubble, straw, and left-over sheath tissue). Sclerotia are extremely resistant to adverse environmental conditions (desiccation, cold, heat, anaerobic paddy flooding, microbial antagonism) and can remain viable in soil for up to 3-5 years in the absence of a susceptible host crop. In spring, when paddy fields are flooded and rice is transplanted, sclerotia float to the surface of the floodwater due to their low buoyant density; they come into direct physical contact with the submerged or water-level portion of the basal rice leaf sheaths, germinate by producing hyphae that directly penetrate the leaf sheath cuticle (no appressorium formation required), and initiate the first primary infections. Within-farm and within-field secondary spread occurs exclusively via mycelial growth across the surface of adjacent plant tissues: runner hyphae grow from a primary lesion up and down the leaf sheath surface, across the narrow air space between touching tillers, and from one rice tiller to the next adjacent tiller by growing across the surface of the floodwater; plant-to-plant spread is usually limited to 30-100 cm from the initial infection focus in a given growing season, which explains why sheath blight typically appears in distinct, expanding circular patches or 'foci' of infection in a rice field, in contrast to the more uniformly distributed pattern of wind-dispersed rice blast. Secondary spread is strongly favored by high canopy humidity (RH > 85%), warm temperatures (28-32 C, optimum 30 C), dense, lush plant canopies, excessive nitrogen fertilizer application (> 150 kg N/ha), and high plant populations (> 150 tillers/m^2). No major, qualitatively inherited, race-specific sheath blight resistance genes (R genes) have been identified in Oryza sativa to date; all known sources of sheath blight resistance are moderate, partial, horizontal, polygenic quantitative trait loci (QTLs) designated qSBR (quantitative sheath blight resistance) derived from O. sativa subsp. japonica, O. nivara, O. rufipogon, O. officinalis, and O. minuta wild rice accessions. Management of rice sheath blight requires a fully integrated multi-component IPM program because of the absence of major-gene genetic resistance. (1) Cultural practices (the first line of defense): (a) balanced, moderate nitrogen fertilization: apply N at 80-120 kg/ha depending on soil type and cultivar, split into 3-4 split applications (basal, tillering, panicle initiation, heading); avoid single large basal N applications (> 150 kg N/ha) which dramatically increase sheath blight severity by 30-80%. (b) use recommended optimum seeding and transplanting densities (approximately 2-3 seedlings per hill, 20 x 20 cm or 25 x 25 cm spacing = 16-25 hills/m^2) to improve air movement and canopy drying; over-transplanting (> 4 seedlings/hill) increases disease severity significantly. (c) crop rotation: 2-3 year crop rotations with non-host crops such as cotton, maize, soybean, wheat, sweet potato, sunflower, or leguminous fallows reduce soil sclerotial populations by 40-70% compared to continuous rice monocropping. (d) water management: maintain intermittent alternate wetting and drying (AWD) irrigation after maximum tillering rather than continuous deep flooding; AWD reduces canopy relative humidity by 5-10% and reduces sclerotial germination; however, excessive drying increases brown planthopper and whitebacked planthopper populations, so AWD must be balanced against insect pest pressure. (e) tillage: fall moldboard plowing to bury surface sclerotia 15-20 cm deep in the soil profile (where sclerotia are killed by anaerobic soil conditions and soil microorganisms) reduces initial inoculum by 50-60% the following spring; zero-till and minimum-till systems generally have higher sheath blight incidence due to surface accumulation of crop residue and sclerotia. (f) residue management: remove, incorporate deeply, or burn rice straw and stubble residue after harvest in areas where sclerotial populations are very high. (g) use of silicon (Si) fertilization: calcium silicate slag amendment at 2-4 t/ha significantly reduces sheath blight lesion length by 40-60% in Si-deficient soils by increasing mechanical strength and silicification of epidermal cell walls. (2) Genetic resistance: partial quantitative QTL-mediated sheath blight resistance is the most sustainable approach; current high-yielding rice cultivars with moderate qSBR levels include 'Teqing', 'Lemont' (moderately susceptible), 'Jasmine 85' (moderately resistant), 'IR64-Sub1 + qSBR pyramids', 'Swarna + qSBR1, qSBR11', 'Zhenshan 97 pyramids', and many Chinese japonica hybrid rice combinations carrying QTLs from O. minuta and O. rufipogon. Transgenic approaches (overexpression of rice chitinase genes, thaumatin-like proteins, OsWRKY transcription factors, and host-induced gene silencing HIGS of R. solani AG-1 IA essential genes) are under advanced development and have demonstrated 40-85% sheath blight reduction in greenhouse and contained field trials. (3) Predictive forecasting models: the EPIRICE, RICEPEST, and IRRI Sheath Blight Model predict disease risk and schedule fungicide application thresholds based on minimum 7-day average temperature > 25 C, minimum average canopy RH > 85%, > 90 tillers per m^2, and plant N content > 3.0% at maximum tillering. (4) Chemical fungicide programs: where sheath blight risk exceeds economic threshold levels, 1-2 well-timed fungicide applications are generally sufficient. The most effective and widely used fungicide groups against R. solani (based on IRRI, CAAS, NRRI, and USDA trials) are: (a) FRAC 7 SDHI (succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor): fluxapyroxad, boscalid, isofetamid, pydiflumetofen, benzovindiflupyr, and especially the latest SDHI solatenol (the most active SDHI against sheath blight to date); SDHIs are the current gold-standard curative + protectant class providing 60-85% control. (b) FRAC 3 DMI triazoles: tebuconazole, propiconazole, difenoconazole, prothioconazole, mefentrifluconazole, ipconazole; good protectant + 2-3 day curative activity; widely used in tank-mix with SDHI and multi-site partners. (c) FRAC 11 QoI (strobilurins): azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, kresoxim-methyl, coumoxystrobin; excellent protectant + translaminar activity; QoI resistance (Cyt b G143A) in R. solani AG-1 IA has been reported in some regions since 2018, so QoIs are always alternated or tank-mixed with non-QoI modes of action. (d) FRAC M3 multi-site contact protectants: mancozeb, maneb, metiram, propineb, chlorothalonil; backbone zero-resistance-risk tank-mix partners. (e) FRAC 2 MBC fungicides (benomyl, carbendazim, thiophanate-methyl): historically very effective, but MBC resistance is now > 95% in most Asian and South American R. solani AG-1 IA populations since the late 1990s, so use is strongly discouraged. (f) FRAC 12 phenylpyrroles (fludioxonil) + FRAC 9 cyprodinil premixes: excellent protectant activity against sclerotial germination. Standard application timings for best sheath blight control: spray 1 at maximum tillering (protectant against initial basal infection), spray 2 at late booting to 10% heading (curative + protectant against critical panicle sheath infection at heading; this second heading-time spray protects the most yield-relevant tissues). In organic rice production, the only moderately effective biological and biorational treatments are: (1) Bacillus subtilis B-916 and B. amyloliquefaciens FZB42 (commercial formulations); (2) Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf-1, Pf-5 and Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain 7NSK2 rhizobacteria; (3) Trichoderma harzianum, T. viride, T. atroviride, and T. asperelloides soil amendments and foliar sprays; (4) Streptomyces hygroscopicus and S. lydicus actinomycetes; (5) botanical extracts (neem oil/azadirachtin, Reynoutria sachalinensis giant knotweed extract, Yucca schidigera saponin extracts, and Laminaria digitata seaweed extracts). (6) Soil application of dry neem cake (250 kg/ha) and mustard cake (300 kg/ha) at the time of final puddling and transplanting reduces sclerotial germination by 30-45%. Overall, organic programs typically achieve 30-55% sheath blight reduction compared to untreated controls, compared to 60-85% reduction from the best conventional fungicide programs. (5) Biological control and microbial antagonists: extensive ICAR-NRRI and IRRI research has identified combination seed treatment + soil application + foliar spray protocols based on multi-strain consortia of T. asperellum + B. amyloliquefaciens + P. fluorescens which provide 45-65% sheath blight reduction and simultaneously suppress rice stem nematode and bacterial blight under moderate disease pressure.
